items.stem: Explain what is meant by diffusion of responsibility.
items.answer: When several bystanders are present, the responsibility to help is spread among them, so each person feels less obligated to act and assumes someone else will help.
items.markingKey: 1 mark spread among bystanders; 1 mark each less likely to act [2]

items.stem: In a busy market in Cairo, an elderly man falls and drops his shopping. Many people walk past before Ines stops to help. Use diffusion of responsibility to explain why many people walked past.
items.answer: With many bystanders, each person assumed someone else would help, so they felt less personal responsibility.
items.markingKey: 1 mark shared responsibility; 1 mark applied [2]

items.stem: Evaluate Piliavin et al.’s (1969) subway Samaritan study in terms of one strength and one weakness.
items.answer: Strength (ecological validity): The study took place on a real New York subway train with ordinary passengers who did not know they were being studied, so their helping behaviour was natural. Weakness (controls): As a field experiment, the researchers could not control the number or type of passengers in each carriage, so extraneous variables may have affected helping. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: Explain the cost–reward model of helping.
items.answer: Seeing a victim creates unpleasant arousal; the bystander reduces it by choosing the response with the lowest net cost, weighing the costs of helping (effort, danger, disgust) against the costs of not helping (guilt, blame).
items.markingKey: 1 mark arousal; 1 mark weighing costs [2]

items.stem: In a busy market in Cape Town, an elderly man falls and drops his shopping. Many people walk past before Nadia stops to help. (a) Use diffusion of responsibility to explain why many people walked past. (b) Use the cost–reward model to explain why Nadia helped.
items.answer: (a) With many bystanders, each person assumed someone else would help, so they felt less personal responsibility. (b) For Nadia the costs of helping (a few minutes) were low and the costs of not helping (guilt, seeing him hurt) were high, so helping reduced arousal at the least cost.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark shared responsibility; 1 mark applied [2] (b) 1 mark costs of helping; 1 mark costs of not helping [2]

items.stem: Evaluate Piliavin et al.’s (1969) subway Samaritan study in terms of two strengths and two weaknesses. At least one of your evaluation points must be about ethics.
items.answer: Strength (sample size): About 4450 passengers were observed over 103 trials, a large and varied sample that increases generalisability to subway users. Strength (cost-reward model): The results (more help for the cane victim) support the cost-reward model, which gives a useful explanation of when people help. Weakness (controls): As a field experiment, the researchers could not control the number or type of passengers in each carriage, so extraneous variables may have affected helping. Weakness (ethics): Passengers did not consent, were deceived into thinking someone had collapsed, could have been distressed and were not debriefed. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: Evaluate Piliavin et al.’s (1969) subway Samaritan study, including a discussion of standardisation.
items.answer: Strength (standardisation): The victim always collapsed about 70 seconds after the train left the station, in the same area of the carriage, and behaved in the same way, so the trials were comparable. Strength (cost-reward model): The results (more help for the cane victim) support the cost-reward model, which gives a useful explanation of when people help. Weakness (reliability): The two observers recorded many details at once in a crowded carriage, so some behaviour may have been missed and inter-rater reliability could not be fully checked. Weakness (controls): As a field experiment, the researchers could not control the number or type of passengers in each carriage, so extraneous variables may have affected helping. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.

items.stem: Describe the procedure of Piliavin et al.’s study.
items.answer: Teams of four students (a victim, a model and two female observers) boarded New York subway trains. About 70 seconds after the train left a station, the male victim collapsed, either carrying a cane (ill) or smelling of alcohol (drunk). Observers recorded how many passengers helped, how quickly, and their sex, race and location. In some trials a model helped after about 70 or 150 seconds if no one else had.
items.markingKey: 1 mark setting/team; 1 mark collapse and conditions; 1 mark observations recorded; 1 mark model [4]

items.stem: Describe the results of Piliavin et al.’s study.
items.answer: The cane victim received spontaneous help in 62 of 65 trials (95%) and the drunk victim in 19 of 38 (50%); help for the cane victim usually came within seconds; 90% of first helpers were male; there was a slight same-race effect for the drunk victim; there was no diffusion of responsibility.
items.markingKey: 1 mark cane/drunk percentages; 1 mark speed; 1 mark sex or race; 1 mark no diffusion [4]

items.stem: Explain why the victim collapsed in the “critical area” of the carriage.
items.answer: So that all trials were standardised and passengers in the critical area (closest to the victim) could be compared with those in the adjacent area.
items.markingKey: 1 mark standardisation; 1 mark comparison of areas [2]

items.stem: Discuss whether field experiments are more useful than laboratory experiments in social psychology.
items.answer: Arguments for: Piliavin et al. observed real helping on a subway with high ecological validity. Participants did not know they were being studied, avoiding demand characteristics. Arguments against: Less control over extraneous variables, such as the number of passengers. Ethical problems: no consent or debriefing. Laboratory studies such as Milgram allow precise control. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.

items.stem: To what extent do you agree that helping behaviour is best explained by the cost–reward model?
items.answer: Arguments for: The cane victim was helped in 95% of trials and the drunk victim in 50%, consistent with higher costs of helping a drunk person. Arousal created by seeing a victim is reduced by helping or leaving. Arguments against: People also help because of empathy or personal norms. The study did not measure passengers’ arousal or thought processes directly. Situational and individual factors such as race and gender also played a part. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.

items.stem: In an ethical field experiment in Auckland, a researcher dropped a pile of books in a shopping centre while either wearing a plaster cast or not. Over 6 trials per condition, the number of passers-by (out of 10) who helped was recorded. Table: Passers-by who helped (out of 10) — Sling (injured): 5, 4, 5, 7, 8, 6. No sling: 6, 3, 10, 4, 3, 3. (a) Calculate the median score for the sling (injured) condition. (b) The standard deviation for the sling (injured) condition was 1.47 and for the no sling condition was 2.79. Explain what these values show. (c) To what extent do these results support the prediction that a researcher wearing a sling will receive help from more passers-by than a researcher without a sling? Use the data in your answer. (d) Suggest one improvement to this study and explain how it would improve the validity or reliability of the results.
items.answer: (a) 5.5 (b) The no sling condition has the larger standard deviation, so its scores are more spread out around the mean; the other condition’s scores are more consistent. (c) Mean for sling (injured) = 5.8 and no sling = 4.8; the direction of the difference matches the prediction, but the scores in the two conditions overlap (ranges 4 and 7) and the sample is small (n = 6 per condition), so the results only partly support it; a statistical test would be needed to show the difference is significant. (d) Use a larger sample with more participants in each condition, so that anomalous individuals have less effect and the results are more reliable and generalisable.

items.stem: In an ethical field experiment in Seoul, a researcher dropped a pile of books in a shopping centre while either wearing a plaster cast or not. Over 10 trials per condition, the number of passers-by (out of 10) who helped was recorded. Table: Passers-by who helped (out of 10) — Sling (injured): 6, 8, 0, 8, 8, 6, 6, 6, 6, 7. No sling: 2, 3, 3, 5, 5, 5, 3, 4, 5, 4. (a) Calculate the percentage of participants in the no sling condition who scored 5 or more. Show your working. (b) Explain why the median may be a better measure of central tendency than the mean for the sling (injured) condition. (c) Using the mean scores, state one conclusion that can be drawn from these results. (d) To what extent do these results support the prediction that a researcher wearing a sling will receive help from more passers-by than a researcher without a sling? Use the data in your answer. (e) Suggest one improvement to this study and explain how it would improve the validity or reliability of the results.
items.answer: (a) 40% (b) The score of 0 is an extreme score (outlier) compared with the rest of the sling (injured) data; the mean is distorted by it, but the median is not affected by extreme values, so it is more representative. (c) The sling (injured) condition had a higher mean (6.1) than the no sling condition (3.9), suggesting that people are more likely to help someone who appears injured. (d) Mean for sling (injured) = 6.1 and no sling = 3.9; the direction of the difference matches the prediction, but the scores in the two conditions overlap (ranges 8 and 3) and the sample is small (n = 10 per condition), so the results only partly support it; a statistical test would be needed to show the difference is significant. (e) Use a larger sample with more participants in each condition, so that anomalous individuals have less effect and the results are more reliable and generalisable.
items.markingKey: (a) 4 out of 10 participants scored 5 or more: 4 ÷ 10 × 100 = 40%. 1 mark working; 1 mark answer [2] (b) 1 mark: identifies the outlier (0); 1 mark: mean distorted / median unaffected by extreme scores [2] (c) 1 mark: conclusion about the effect of the IV on the DV; 1 mark: supported with the means [2] (d) 1 mark: uses both means; 1 mark: judgement about direction; 1 mark: limitation such as overlap of scores, small sample or no statistical test [3] (e) 1 mark: improvement; 1 mark: how to do it; 1 mark: effect on validity/reliability explained [3]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) In a revision session, a student says: “Piliavin et al.’s findings can be generalised to all countries and all time periods.” Is this correct? Explain your answer. (b) Explain how Piliavin et al.’s results support the cost–reward model.

items.stem: Assess the view that helping behaviour is best explained by the cost–reward model. In your answer, you may refer to situational and individual explanations, diffusion of responsibility and ecological validity.
items.answer: Arguments for: The cane victim was helped in 95% of trials and the drunk victim in 50%, consistent with higher costs of helping a drunk person. Arousal created by seeing a victim is reduced by helping or leaving. Arguments against: People also help because of empathy or personal norms. The study did not measure passengers’ arousal or thought processes directly. Situational and individual factors such as race and gender also played a part. Conclusion: a supported judgement weighing the evidence on both sides.

Middle band: relevant knowledge with some evaluation, but one side or the conclusion is underdeveloped. Lower band: limited, mostly descriptive answer with little evaluation.

items.stem: Discuss the strengths and weaknesses of Piliavin et al.’s (1969) subway Samaritan study. Include at least one point about reliability.
items.answer: Strength (ecological validity): The study took place on a real New York subway train with ordinary passengers who did not know they were being studied, so their helping behaviour was natural. Strength (cost-reward model): The results (more help for the cane victim) support the cost-reward model, which gives a useful explanation of when people help. Weakness (controls): As a field experiment, the researchers could not control the number or type of passengers in each carriage, so extraneous variables may have affected helping. Weakness (reliability): The two observers recorded many details at once in a crowded carriage, so some behaviour may have been missed and inter-rater reliability could not be fully checked. Conclusion: a reasoned judgement about the overall value of the study.
items.markingKey: Levels of response. Top band: strengths and weaknesses are accurate, well explained and clearly linked to the study, the named issue is discussed, the answer is well organised and reaches a conclusion. Middle band: points are mostly accurate but one side is less developed or links to the study are general. Lower band: points are identified but brief, generic or one-sided. Description of the procedure without evaluation receives little credit.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why the victim collapsed in the “critical area” of the carriage. (b) Describe the procedure of Piliavin et al.’s study.
items.answer: (a) So that all trials were standardised and passengers in the critical area (closest to the victim) could be compared with those in the adjacent area. (b) Teams of four students (a victim, a model and two female observers) boarded New York subway trains. About 70 seconds after the train left a station, the male victim collapsed, either carrying a cane (ill) or smelling of alcohol (drunk). Observers recorded how many passengers helped, how quickly, and their sex, race and location. In some trials a model helped after about 70 or 150 seconds if no one else had.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark standardisation; 1 mark comparison of areas [2] (b) 1 mark setting/team; 1 mark collapse and conditions; 1 mark observations recorded; 1 mark model [4]
